upcoming.title: 3.14.0-rc.0 / 2026-08-06
upcoming.description:
- [CHANGE] API: Deprecate the `stats` query parameter of `/api/v1/query` and `/api/v1/query_range` for values other than `true` and `all`. Other values still enable basic statistics but now return a deprecation warning; they will be rejected in the next major release. #19124
- [CHANGE] API: `/api/v1/status/config` now correctly shows `separator: ""` and `replacement: ""` in relabel configs when explicitly set to empty, instead of omitting them. #18653
- [CHANGE] Discovery/Hetzner: Drop the `__meta_hetzner_datacenter` label for `hcloud` targets, following its removal from the Hetzner Cloud API. #19269
- [CHANGE] PromQL: Enable duration expressions by default. The `promql-duration-expr` feature flag is now a no-op. #19033
- [CHANGE] PromQL: Promote `first_over_time` to stable. It no longer requires the `promql-experimental-functions` feature flag. #19093
- [FEATURE] Discovery: Add Oracle Cloud Infrastructure compute service discovery (`oci_sd_configs`). #18919
- [FEATURE] PromQL: A

upcoming.title: Native Histograms
upcoming.description:
This milestone is mostly about merging the new native histograms (AKA sparse histograms AKA high-res histograms) into the main branch (and hide it behind a feature flag), and only after that about declaring native histograms a stable feature (ultimately no-op'ing the feature flag). Therefore, the priorities have a slightly different meaning (because the issues do not affect the released Prometheus versions before we merge to the main branch):
* **P0:** Prometheus, if built from the sparsehistogram branch, doesn't work properly until this is fixed.
* **P1:** We must fix this before merging to main (e.g. Prometheus might not work properly even if the feature flag is not set)
* **P2:** We can merge to main without this but we need to fix this to declare Histograms stable.
* **P3:** Nice to have. Can be introduced later without a breaking change.
* **P4:** The future! Do not focus on this for now. (Labeled as Pmaybe.)

signals.title: promql: native histogram optimization incorrectly skips buckets when intermediate operators need them
signals.text: ### Description The native histogram optimization `detectHistogramStatsDecoding` incorrectly enables bucket-skipping (`SkipHistogramBuckets = true`) for `VectorSelector`s even when intermediate operators in the AST require those buckets. For example, in the query `histogram_count(m1 + m2)`, the binary operator `+` needs the buckets of `m1` and `m2` to correctly merge them (especially if they have different schemas or bucket boundaries). However, the current implementation of `detectHistogramStatsDecoding` walks up the path and, if it finds `histogram_count` anywhere above the selector, it enables the optimization, leading to incorrect results because the binary operator receives histograms without buckets. ### Repoduction Steps 1. execute a query like `histogram_count(series1 + series2)` where `series1` and `series2` are native histograms. 2. the result is incorrect or potentially causes issues in the binary operator because buckets were skipped at the storage/iterator level.

signals.title: promql/parser: parentheses around a plain duration literal are lost on round-trip
signals.text: Note: I've generated this issue with Claude Opus 4.7 after using it to verify the issue. While reviewing #18768 I noticed that `(N)` inside a duration-expression position (offset, range bracket) is dropped on `Expr.String()` round-trip when N reduces to a single `*NumberLiteral`. Wrapping a multi-term `*DurationExpr` survives because `*DurationExpr` has a `Wrapped` field; `*NumberLiteral` has no such field. ### Reproduction With `ExperimentalDurationExpr: true`: #### Cases that lose parentheses | Input | `Expr.String()` | |------------------------|------------------| | `foo offset (5)` | `foo offset 5s` | | `foo offset +(5)` | `foo offset 5s` | | `foo offset -(5)` | `foo offset -5s` | | `foo offset (5m)` | `foo offset 5m` | | `foo[(5s)]` | `foo[5s]` | #### Cases that round-trip correctly (for reference) | Input | `Expr.String()` | |--------------------------|--------------------------| | `(5)` | `(5)` | | `-(5)` | `-(5)` | | `+(5)` | `+(5)` | | `(5) + 1` | `(5) + 1` | | `foo offset (5m + 1m)` | `foo offset (5m + 1m)` | | `foo offset -(5m + 1m)` | `foo offset -(5m + 1m)` | | `foo[(5s + 1s)]` | `foo[(5s + 1s)]` | Pure-scalar contexts use `*ParenExpr`, which prints its own parens. Duration-expression contexts with a `*DurationExpr` payload preserve parens via the `Wrapped` field. The mismatch is only when the payload is a single `*NumberLiteral`. ### Notes This pre-dates #18768. That PR fixes a panic on `foo offset -(5)` but inherits this round-trip limitation, which is why I'm filing it separately.

signals.text: ### What did you do? Read through discovery/ionos/server.go while looking at the AWS SD nil-guard fixes (#19184, #19374) to see if other SD implementations have the same issue. ### What did you expect to see? Optional fields being omitted from the label set when absent, matching the guard pattern already used elsewhere in the same file (e.g. `server.Properties.BootCdrom`) and in other SDs. ### What did you see instead? `refresh()` builds part of the label set from a struct literal that dereferences several pointer fields with no nil check: ```go labels := model.LabelSet{ model.AddressLabel: model.LabelValue(addr), serverAvailabilityZoneLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.AvailabilityZone), serverCPUFamilyLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.CpuFamily), serverServersIDLabel: model.LabelValue(*servers.Id), serverIDLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Id), serverIPLabel: model.LabelValue(join(ips, metaLabelSeparator)), serverLifecycleLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Metadata.State), serverNameLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.Name), serverStateLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.VmState), serverTypeLabel: model.LabelValue(*server.Properties.Type), } ``` All of `Id`, `AvailabilityZone`, `CpuFamily`, `Name`, `VmState`, `Type` (on `ServerProperties`), plus `Id` on `Server`/`Servers`, and `Metadata`/`State` (on `DatacenterElementMetadata`), are declared as pointers with `omitempty` in the IONOS SDK (github.com/ionos-cloud/sdk-go/v6), so the API can legitimately omit any of them. If it does, this panics. There's no `recover()` in discovery/, so it takes down the whole process, same as the EC2 case in #19374. ### System information Code inspection against `main`.

signals.title: tsdb [PERF]: optimize head ShardedPostings with shard bucket postings
signals.text: `ShardedPostings` on head previously filtered by doing a `stripeSeries.getByID` lookup for every input posting so it could read the cached shard hash. On large heads this makes query sharding pay a per-series map lookup once per shard for every queried postings list. This PR adds a head shard bucket postings index. When sharding is enabled, each series is inserted into a bucket derived from its stable shard hash. For power-of-two shard counts, `ShardedPostings` intersects the input postings with the relevant bucket postings instead of resolving every series through `getByID`. The bucket index preserves the existing modulo-sharding contract: - Power-of-two shard counts use the bucket index. - Power-of-two shard counts larger than the bucket count use the matching bucket, then lazily resolve the intersected candidate refs for the final shard-hash filter. - Non-power-of-two shard counts fall back to the generic per-series filtering path. - The bucket index can be disabled with `ShardedPostingsBuckets < 0`, while keeping sharding enabled through the generic fallback. This also adds the optional reader-scoped `ShardedAllPostingsReader` interface for callers that need all head postings for a shard, plus `HeadOptions.ShardedPostingsBuckets` and `Options.ShardedPostingsBuckets` so embedders can tune or disable the bucket index. Dirty bucket repairs replace full bucket slices. Churn-heavy embedders can opt into a bounded `ShardedPostingsBufferRecycler` and share it across DBs or Heads through `Options` or `HeadOptions`. Displaced buffers become reusable only after every index reader that could still observe them closes. Retention is bounded by the configured byte budget and 128 idle buffers; constructing the recycler with a zero budget disables it. Head repair counters and recycler hit, miss, eviction, rejection, retained, and pending-retirement metrics make the allocation rate and retained memory observable. The implementation keeps bucket refs sorted for efficient intersection. Normal series creation appends in order; out-of-order appends mark the affected suffix dirty. On read, a copied bucket is sorted in full if the dirty region begins before the midpoint; otherwise only the necessary suffix is sorted. Candidate buckets are captured independently, and returned postings remain valid after unlock for their index reader's lifetime because existing slice contents are not mutated. A separate per-bucket replacement mutex serializes sorting and removal without blocking clean readers or appends. Dirty sorting and survivor rebuilding prepare replacement slices outside the main bucket lock, carry over concurrent append tails, and briefly re-lock to install the result. Deleted series carry their shard hash into bucket removal, so GC rebuilds only affected buckets. Bucket entries are ref-only. Earlier experiments stored an aligned shard-hash sidecar for over-bucket shard counts, but that added measurable creation-path overhead. The current implementation keeps the cheap exact bucket path and handles over-bucket shard counts by intersecting first, then doing lazy shard-hash lookups only over the reduced candidate set. Bucket-backed `ShardedPostings` routes through `index.Intersect`. Earlier experiments compared this against a custom sequential shard-filter strategy, and `index.Intersect` won across shard counts `{2,4,8,16,64,128,256}` for both flat and merge-tree inputs. #### Benchmarks Environment: `darwin/arm64`, Apple M4 Pro. Comparisons used `go test -benchmem -count=6`. Benchmarked comparison base: `prometheus/main` `7070104b3485ae8999d6e77f9c654df4af42b1d6`; main-equivalent benchmarked branch revision: `6b8979e47d9dd7213dec7ff089e8b94362a896ce`. The baseline was `prometheus/main` patched only with the benchmark harness used for this comparison so both sides exposed the same benchmark names. Remove-path and branch-only diagnostic measurements were captured at `3cb990234ce81bb10648f2b453e9e624d34ab565`, except for the fallback all-postings comparison refreshed at `f3dead9ceb09d7625852b461b9cb9f35f140938a`. The current branch head is `148e128f00780c81ea9e25f16a8f9a167c83362e`; it retains the bucket-routing query path and adds reader-scoped `ShardedAllPostings` plus opt-in repair-buffer recycling. The main-equivalent tables remain revision-pinned evidence for the bucket-index query path, while the remove-path table is explicitly historical and the current lock-contention and recycling measurements are summarized below. Benchmark names were reorganized after these measurements. Historical benchstat output remains verbatim; current names map as follows: - `ShardBucketDirtySort` -> `ShardBucketPostings_DirtySort` - `ShardBucketPostingsFootprint` -> `ShardBucketPostings_Footprint` - `ShardBucketPostings/add` -> `ShardBucketPostings_Add` - `ShardBucketPostings/shardPostings` -> `ShardBucketPostings_PostingsFor` - `ShardBucketPostings/remove` -> `ShardBucketPostings_Remove` - `ShardBucketPostings/concurrentRemoveRead` -> `ShardBucketPostings_ConcurrentRemoveRead` Later benchmark cleanup removed the redundant `shardCount=256` cases from `ShardBucketPostings_PostingsFor` and `ShardBucketPostings_ConcurrentRemoveRead`, and the redundant `dense/churn=1/3` deletion pattern. Revision-pinned historical benchstat output below retains those cases. ##### Dirty-repair buffer recycling `BenchmarkShardBucketPostings_DirtyRepairBufferReuse` repeatedly repairs a 65,536-ref dirty bucket. A warm recycler eliminates the 524,416-byte repair-buffer allocation on every operation: benchmark-visible memory falls from about 520.1 KiB/op to 80-81 B/op while total allocations remain 3/op. The concurrent recycler benchmark measures 438-463 ns/op and 0 allocs/op. The command was `go test ./tsdb -run '^$' -bench '^(BenchmarkShardBucketPostings_DirtyRepairBufferReuse|BenchmarkShardedPostingsBufferRecycler_ConcurrentGetPut)$' -benchmem -count=6`. A process-level Mimir benchmark exercises 128 concurrent active-series shard requests against all 128 dirty buckets through both `ShardedAllPostings` and selective `ShardedPostings`. It compares recycling disabled with a 16 MiB shared recycler. Each result below is six single-operation samples from `go test ./pkg/ingester -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkIngester_ActiveSeriesFullFanout$' -benchtime=1x -benchmem -count=6`: ```console median repair buffer allocs/op B/op sec/op ShardedAllPostings/dirty-cold 128 -> 48 (-62.50%) 16.53 -> 10.07 MiB no significant change ShardedAllPostings/dirty-warm 128 -> 0 (-100.00%) 16.53 -> 6.14 MiB no significant change ShardedPostings/dirty-cold 128 -> 62.5 (-51.17%) 11.17 -> 5.86 MiB no significant change ShardedPostings/dirty-warm 128 -> 0 (-100.00%) 11.17 -> 0.78 MiB -23.80% (p=0.004) ``` The warm cases retain 128 buffers using 12 MiB, serve all 128 repairs from the recycler, and finish with no pending-retirement buffers. Clean-path timing has no significant change, and the clean selective path has no significant change in B/op or allocs/op. ##### Current dirty-sort append contention `BenchmarkShardBucketPostings_ConcurrentDirtySort` uses deterministic synchronization points to start an append while a dirty replacement is being prepared. The initial lock-scope comparison used the same benchmark harness before and after moving sorting outside the main bucket lock: ```console locked sort unlocked replacement append latency p50 1.08254 ms 12.94 us -98.80% append latency p99 1.41775 ms 89.06 us -93.72% ``` The final tail-carry comparison forces more concurrent appends than `replacementTailHeadroom`, exercising replacement-slice growth rather than the normal reserved-capacity path: ```console before current append latency p50 14.291 us 125 ns -99.13% append latency p99 24.250 us 562.5 ns -97.68% ``` Allocation counts were unchanged in both comparisons. Moving overflow-tail growth out of the main lock increased aggregate benchmark time by 3.88% in the tail-growth row and 6.68% in the normal-sort row; normal-sort append p99 changed from 291 ns to 625 ns and remains sub-microsecond. This is the measured tradeoff for removing the 14-24 us append stalls in the overflow path. signals.title: promql: add per-query toggling of Start Timestamp processing
signals.text: #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #18969 #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). ```release-notes [FEATURE] API: Allow overriding PromQL Start Timestamp processing on a per-query basis using the `use_start_timestamps` query parameter or `X-Prometheus-Use-Start-Timestamps` HTTP header. ``` ### Summary This adds a per-query override for PromQL Start Timestamp (ST) processing instead of always using the global `UseStartTimestamps` engine flag. The value is read from the `X-Prometheus-Start-Timestamps` HTTP header. If the header is not set, it falls back to the `start_timestamps` query parameter. This makes it easier to test or debug installations where some metrics have incorrect start timestamps. Users can enable ST for a single query before turning it on globally, or temporarily disable it for a query even if the global flag is enabled to compare results. Recording rules (`rules/manager.go`) still pass `nil` query options, so they continue using the global engine configuration. ### Usage ```bash # Enable ST processing for a single query curl -H "X-Prometheus-Use-Start-Timestamps: true" \ "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(my_counter[5m])" # Disable ST processing for a single query curl -H "X-Prometheus-Use-Start-Timestamps: false" \ "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(my_counter[5m])" ```

signals.title: tsdb/index: fix data race in memposting
signals.text: Fixes: #15317 ## What This refactors `MemPostings` to safely handle concurrent readers and out-of-order insertions by tracking which portion of each postings list may already be visible to readers. Instead of always copying an entire postings list when repairing an ordering violation, the implementation now performs in-place repairs whenever it is safe, falling back to copying only when readers could observe the modified region. The change also introduces sharded read tracking, preserves the fast path for in-order appends, restores regression tests, and fixes the race condition that could cause queries to return incorrect series. ## Why Previously, `MemPostings` repaired ordering violations by modifying postings lists in place after readers had already obtained references to them, introducing a data race and allowing readers to observe incorrectly ordered postings. An earlier fix resolved the race by copying the entire postings list on every repair, but this caused excessive memory allocations and was reverted due to poor performance. signals.title: Avoid locking HEAD shards when running gc
signals.text: After HEAD writes a block it runs GC to prune series that no longer have any chunks in HEAD, this fully locks each HEAD shard while it's being scanned for series to prune. That locked shard blocks all queries (because it's a write lock) and it can be visible on metrics as a sudden spike in queued queries. The more series we have in Prometheus the more visible this is. Often there are very few series to actually prune, so most of this time is spent iterating over all series, the more series the longer each shard scan takes (since the number of shards is static). Try to avoid this blocking by doing prunes in two phases: - first iterate under a read lock and find series to prune - then, if there are any series found, do a second loop over identified series and prune these under a write lock This way we only lock each shard to the actual pruning, not for scanning. It's safe because series can only receive samples, they can't become empty, while we're running a GC. <!-- - Please give your PR a title in the form "area: short description". signal.title: promql: native histogram optimization incorrectly skips buckets when intermediate operators need them
signal.text: ### Description The native histogram optimization `detectHistogramStatsDecoding` incorrectly enables bucket-skipping (`SkipHistogramBuckets = true`) for `VectorSelector`s even when intermediate operators in the AST require those buckets. For example, in the query `histogram_count(m1 + m2)`, the binary operator `+` needs the buckets of `m1` and `m2` to correctly merge them (especially if they have different schemas or bucket boundaries). However, the current implementation of `detectHistogramStatsDecoding` walks up the path and, if it finds `histogram_count` anywhere above the selector, it enables the optimization, leading to incorrect results because the binary operator receives histograms without buckets. ### Repoduction Steps 1. execute a query like `histogram_count(series1 + series2)` where `series1` and `series2` are native histograms. 2. the result is incorrect or potentially causes issues in the binary operator because buckets were skipped at the storage/iterator level.

signal.title: promql/parser: preserve parentheses around duration literals
signal.text: #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #18770 #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes [BUGFIX] PromQL: Preserve parentheses around duration literals on Expr.String() round-trip. ``` `paren_duration_expr` only set `Wrapped` on `*DurationExpr`, so a parenthesised `*NumberLiteral` (`foo offset (5)`, `foo[(5s)]`) was flattened by `Expr.String()`. This wraps a parenthesised number in a unary-plus `*DurationExpr` with `Wrapped: true`, matching how `+(5*2)` already survives. Unary `+(5)` / `-(5)` go through the same path. @krajorama @roidelapluie @vpranckaitis
